utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber has considered whether -- how much time it would grant for your re-examination. I don't know, let me first ask what you have on your mind at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I tried to be really as short as possible, but at least two hours. Yesterday we had that videolink that and we had many problems with the recording and with translating. We have to go through many things. There are many holes in the transcript as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider after one hour and please focus then on the most important matters whether it should grant a second hour. We have, apart from some other thoughts we have on the matter, but apart from that, there's also a very practical matter that your next witness we have this week the videolink, and therefore, I take it that we would like to conclude the evidence of the next witness as well this week. That means by tomorrow. So would you please be very focussed and after the first break we'll consider whether more time will be granted. Could we establish whether the videolink is functioning? Could the representative of the Registry at the other side confirm that he hears as well and that he sees us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. Yes, I confirm that I can hear and see you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the videolink room. And may I take it, as yesterday, there's only one other person in that room, that is the technician?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That's correct, Your Honour. Yes, since yesterday, that's been the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And please proceed to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Basara.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Lukic will now re-examine you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Basara.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today we will have to move on a bit faster because our time is limited so do try to give answers that are as short as possible. When you were asked -- actually, maybe it would be faster. I've already indicated there were problems with the transcript. I'm just going to say something to the Trial Chamber now, Mr. Basara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 34398 is the transcript page. This is what was recorded. In line 2 and further on, I quote: [In English] "Based on my orders that I brought the brigade in with the task of preparing conflict in the territory of municipality of Sanski Most." What the Defence heard at that time was "preventing conflict."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the correct way to do is to ask the witness can you repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was my dilemma: Should I hurry up or go step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The best way of dealing with it, of course, if the witness misspoke he's the one who should correct. If it is a wrong recording you should have verified that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S it is completely two words, two different words so we think it in translation. Preventing, preparing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but the sound can sound similar. In B/C/S, it cannot. But I can ask or it's too late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look. Yes, you should ask the witness, Mr. -- there's the only thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Basara, what was your task when you came to the area of Sanski Most? What was the task that you were given?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade was given the task to prevent conflicts between Serbs, Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have P2865 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for that, I don't know whether you can see that on the screen over there or whether you're given hard copies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, on the screen, can you see that document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see this order from the corps to the division.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown the last paragraph under number 1 where it says: "Establish full co-operation with the organs of government in Sanski Most municipality and co-ordination with TO units and police units."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the date that Mr. Lukic mentioned. He is speaking too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, the interpreters are asking you to slow down and they missed the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, since it's a videolink I cannot follow English channel so I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's why I draw your attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it's -- I mentioned April the 1st, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, sir, your answer hasn't been recorded. Please tell us again. What was the ethnicity of the man who headed the TO in Sanski Most at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, it was Captain Nijaz Halilovic, an ethnic Muslim, who headed the TO Staff, and he told me that he had declared himself to be a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Same question was put in relation to document P7324. This is what I'm going ask you: To what extent were you geared towards civilian authorities and to what extent were they geared towards you in 1992 in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was mostly geared towards the civilian authorities in terms of manning the brigade. That is to say, during mobilisation in co-operation with the Secretariat for National Defence. They had nothing special to do with me. It wasn't that I had any special requests received from them to give them some kind of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can we now briefly look at P23465, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a -- a very high number, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: P2365. [Interpretation] In relation to this document, we wish to inform the Trial Chamber that although the translation has been uploaded, even this revised translation is not right, so we really have to look at this with the OTP and they noticed some mistakes even in the revised translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Rasula -- actually, Mr. Basara, I would like to ask you: How did you find out that Rasula and Vrkes went to see General Talic to ask for your replacement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Talic told me and I heard people talking about that from others who had more contact with Rasula and Vrkes, that they were not satisfied with my work and that they went to Banja Luka to see Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there anything specific in regard to their complaints or was it just in general terms?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing specific. I can just tell you about a clash I had with Rasula, but I can tell you one thing. When Talic told me that they had come to ask him to replace me, and then he said to me, Leave it as it is, go on working the way you've been working so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P3294, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document was shown to you. This is Nedjeljko Rasula's diary. At least that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the pages that were shown to you by the OTP; 22 in English and in the B/C/S version, page 20. We need the very top of the left part of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is written here is that this is a meeting held on 20th April 1992 and it says: "With General Talic, Colonel Basara, Major Zeljaja, representatives of the SDS, SDA, and the HDZ."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't think we are on the right page in English. Perhaps it's the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Obviously. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We still are not on the right page, I'm afraid. It should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The date should be on the previous page. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The rest is on this page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The top of the -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 34436 of our transcript, you said that there is a Lieutenant-Colonel Talic and that you think that he's been confused with General Talic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion now is - because I cannot remember at all - that General Talic attended together with me at all, but I do remember that Lieutenant-Colonel Talic did attend. I think his first name is Mustafa or something like that. He came several times to the municipal assembly, and he probably came there in relation to his family, wanting to have his family protected and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of Lieutenant-Colonel Talic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Muslim. And he was serving in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now what is written here further down is attendees. I'm going to read out what was recorded but maybe if you know the full names and surnames you can tell us as well as the ethnicity. Mirzet, do you know who that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. He was president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Redzo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Redzo, president of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we -- could you ask the witness for the full name of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know Mirzet's last name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirzet Karabegovic or Karabeg or something like that, and Redzo is Kurbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim, and they were the main people in the Muslim leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sabic is the next one recorded here. Do you know his first naming and what his ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suad Sabic. He was also a delegate there at the assembly and he was rather influential amongst them, but he was also rather objective in his discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ante is the next one recorded here.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante, I think his last name was Saric or something like that. He was president of the HDZ and during all debates in the Municipal Assembly whenever I took part in the debate, he was the one who supported me the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is Ante's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last one written down here is Vlado. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlado Vrkes. He was present of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nedjeljko Rasula was president of the Crisis Staff. Did he chair meetings of the Crisis Staff when you were present?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then, no. This was not a meeting of the Crisis Staff. Because the Crisis Staff hadn't been established then, because the Municipal Assembly was functioning. Later on the Crisis Staff was established when there was a division of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Precisely. However, when Rasula became president of the Crisis Staff, did he chair meetings of the Crisis Staff that you attended?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While he chaired these meetings, did he keep this diary? Could you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not see that. I could not see him keeping a diary. I just saw Colonel Anicic writing something down all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know at all when Rasula made these entries in his diary?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No insight whatsoever. Because after these meetings, I usually went to my command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Rasula ask for these entries to be checked either by you or somebody else? Do you know about that? Did he familiarize other people, members of the Crisis Staff, with the entries made?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any of this. And I did not have any possibility of any kind of insight into any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P3294. Could we please take a look that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not the one on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. I just checked, yes. Thank you. [Interpretation] We need page 40 in English and page 30 in B/C/S. We need the page on the right in B/C/S. The meeting on the 11th of May, 1992. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us that you did not act on orders from the Crisis Staff. Did the Crisis Staff act on orders that you issued?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not act on orders that I issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said something that was not recorded in the transcript. I don't want to make a mistake, hence I will repeat my question. Did your command or you personally receive decisions or conclusions of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not. We did not receive either conclusions or decisions of the Crisis Staff, and we did not act upon them. That's one thing. Another thing, as we can see from the documents, some of the documents do not have a signature at the bottom proving that they were compiled subsequently. Those that do bear Rasula's signature, there's no distribution list, hence, there is no mention of the 6th Brigade being in receipt of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As an example, we'd like to show the following document to the Chamber of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff. That is 240708. And 1-3, that is 2413. We can see in those documents that they were not sent to the address of the 6th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you referring to a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you should repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: P2407, P2408, and P2413. Thank you, Your Honour, again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, where you said we can see in those documents they were not sent to the address of the 6th Brigade, well, I take it that you cannot see that they were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are traces where those three documents were sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are addressees at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they do not appear among the addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you wanted to say. That's not exactly the same, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This same document, we need the English page 51 and the B/C/S page 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the very bottom of the page, under 1, we have you speaking, Colonel Basara, that is. It is stated the TO has been given the status of an army under a single command. Apparently that was Rasula's note and it was read out to you - just bear with me - it was read out to you by my learned friend Mr. Jeremy at transcript page 34480. I will show you another document in relation to this and the issue of whether the TO was given the status of army on the date that Rasula noted down. We need an 8th June 1992 document for that reason.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Lukic kindly repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] P2414. The first page in both versions, number 6. One of the conclusions reads --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Should the Territorial Defence be abolished and the 6th Brigade reorganised, a manoeuvre unit of company size should be formed from the TO units and the police force of the SJB to carry disarming and other actions in the competence of the SJB. The TO Staff and the SJB are entrusted with this task."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you were not familiar with the conclusion, but do you know whether in June the TO Staff was still in operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly in terms of date and period, but the TO was made part of the brigade at some point, and on that day, although I don't remember what day it was, I appointed new battalion commanders. The previous battalion commanders were replaced by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next, can we please have P2874.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your work yesterday, my learned friend Mr. Jeremy suggested that the Serbs were in favour of separation from the other two peoples, and he showed you this document to that effect. This document was discussed at transcript page 34450 and onwards. Very well. At the bottom of the page in B/C/S, it reads -- there's a sentence to that effect. So it's the last paragraph in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be in English on top of the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It reads: "The constituent Serbian people, who live on around 65 per cent of the area and represent more than 35 per cent of the population of BH, must struggle for complete separation from the Muslim and Croatian peoples and form their own state." It was mentioned in the 1st Krajina Corps command document of 21 May 1995 [as interpreted]. However, in this document, before the part that we can see at the bottom of the page, we also read --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we go back to the previous page in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And before you continue, it's not 1995 but 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were recorded as saying in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I misspoke, I'm not sure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it was mentioned in the 1st Krajina Corps command document. However, in this document, is this document not also a Krajina Corps command document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same document, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It reads in item 1, the fourth line: "Besides the realignments in the spheres of idealogy, politics, and economy, and the system of social value, the general settling of scores has also spread to state territories, which are being redrawn." There is mention made of the influence exerted by other states and the attempt of creating midget states that could be manipulated in this way. My question is this: In terms of efforts for Yugoslavia to survive, were they directed at divisions and separations, or at unity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is, based on my personal work and my desire, as well as my activity, and that is, before the situation in Dobrovoljacka Street, the prevailing opinion was the -- in favour of the preservation of the SFRY and that those republics, which had not seceded and had not been recognised by international factors, to remain as part of that Yugoslavia. However, following Dobrovoljacka Street and the killing of several JNA members, soldiers and officers, there was a change in situation. It was realised that the two peoples could no longer could co-exist, especially Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, for the sake of the record, your quotation lines 12 to 15 I found it in document, but the next two lines, I can't find it -- it's not a complete quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it's summarisation. So I don't read everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. That's only a summary of the following passages of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, around the 21st of May, if you know, if you followed, what was the status of non-Slovenians in Slovenia regarding the issue of Slovenian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information I have, although I did not have extensive contacts there but from what I could hear from the people coming from the area, they stated that they were looking forward to having Serbs removed from their territory, for them to go back to where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether people lost Slovenian citizenship and how long did that process last?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long it lasted but I do know that there are people who lost their citizenship and who were basically prohibited from returning to the territory of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Croatia around the 21st of May, 1992, were the Serbs still a constituent people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our understanding, the Serbs were a constituent people. However, based on the opinion of Croatian authorities, they were not. At that point in time, they were already considered a minority and they were striving to drive them out from Croatian territory so that Serbs are no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, what was the breaking point? You mentioned Dobrovoljacka Street. What was the turning point? When did this change for unity change -- this wish for unity change?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The turning point was Dobrovoljacka Street and the situation in Tuzla when JNA units were withdrawing from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were attacked then, and quite a few members of the JNA were killed. One could understand if it happened as the JNA -- as JNA was coming to the territory, but they were leaving and yet they were killed. They were not placing the Muslim people in danger. And the ones in Tuzla were even without arms. They had surrendered their weapons and yet they were attacked. Next, there was an incident in Kljuc. There was a unit coming from Bosanski Petrovac. It was attacked and four JNA members were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I wanted to say something about P7321 MFI. The Prosecution stated that it received it from the AID agency, AID. On the cover page it is stated that it is the notebook of the pioneers' platoon commander. We don't see that piece of information in the document itself, and we are interested where it came from. In the notebook, according to our lay opinion, there are different handwritings, so we would like to know who made entries and we'd like to hear a Prosecution submission on it. It also reads that it is an excerpt, so we would be interested in who made the selection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this a question to the witness or are you addressing the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm addressing the court, Your Honour. [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps first use the time with the witness. You could either have made any submissions in this respect -- it's all valid points but not perhaps at this moment to address the Court in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to go through him with all of these questions so that's why I'm trying to cut this down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness apparently doesn't know anything about it so, therefore, it would be -- but it's on the record that you still have your concerns about the authenticity of this document and you address that later. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At page of our transcript 34489, lines 10 through 15, you discuss Mahala. Your sentence was left incomplete. It reads in line 15 and I'll quote since there was overlapping of speakers. [In English] "A. Three hours were given to get all of those out who --" [Interpretation] Mr. Basara, what was this that you were talking about when you said that three hours were given.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three hours were given for all of those who do not wish to fight, that is to say, who do not wish to put up resistance when having their weapons taken away they should leave Mahala and go to an area designated for that where there was security so that they would not be under any kind of threat. That means that those who stay on in Mahala were resolved to fight and put up a resistance. That is the essence of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, however incomplete in this specific point the transcript may be, the witness explained this three or four times to us. So, therefore, there could be no doubt as what he would have said if he would have completed that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Basara, the people who went out, where were they put up? Who took care of them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were put up in the area towards Pjevci and that area was secured by parts of units of the 6th Brigade, and there were no casualties there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P4161. Could we please take a look that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Mr. Jeremy, showed you this document of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most of the 19th of June, 1992, and there was a discussion about you being a member of the Crisis Staff. You see, down here, number 7, you are mentioned as a permanent member of the Crisis Staff. The question is whether you have ever received a document informing you that you have become a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received no document informing me that I was a member of the Crisis Staff. Now that I think about it, I cannot even remember that anyone communicated that to me, at all. So I, as brigade commander, for the purpose of information and because of my wish to influence certain matters so that they would evolve in a better way, to my mind, I came to attend these meetings but I did not take part in decision-making there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever accept any such thing? Did you ever accept to be a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never accepted that. As a matter of fact, if I'm allowed to do so, I would like to say that I once had this conflict with Rasula. It had to do with the removal of street names, streets that were named after national heros, partisans, and he said to me, I am issuing an order to that effect and I said on the basis of what, president? We're not under the command of the municipality, and he said, yes, under the command of Karadzic he is the supreme commander, the president of the SDS and I can issue orders to you. I replied sharply to him that he could not give orders because there is a chain of command: Mladic, Talic, brigade and that I am carrying out only orders issued by the 1st Krajina Corps. So Rasula never tried to issue any orders to me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 34471, that is a reference to our transcript, something was not recorded and I'm going to ask you something now and I don't want to confuse you in any way because you probably think that you've already said this but you did say that in line 13 on this page, but it was not recorded in the transcript. Under whose command was the Territorial Defence and the MUP in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the legal organs of the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most. That is to say, when the government was established all the structures were there, all the structures that a municipality should have. So they were under their command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the municipal assembly while it existed and what succeeded that structure.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the take-over when they entered the municipal assembly, then they established all the organs that a municipality should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like us to take a brief look at D79. Again, this is a document of the Crisis Staff of the Serb Municipality of Sanski Most of the 22nd of May, 1992. Number 1, the letter d on the first page. There was a discussion and Judge Moloto asked you something about that. The order was that Colonel Basara and Colonel Anicic should organise the protection of vital facilities and your answer was not fully recorded, so I'd like to ask you now whether you co-operated with Colonel Anicic with regard to this matter.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. I did not co-operate with Colonel Anicic with regard to this matter. As for the facilities, I did not secure them. I only at that time I just had 50 people in the centre of Sanski Most near the warehouse, the arms depot, to protect that facility so that there would not be a conflict in terms of who would take that facility over. Then the president of the Executive Board, Mirza Karabeg, or Mirzet Karabeg as I read just now, children were afraid when they saw soldiers in the street so it would be a good idea for them to withdraw from Sanski Most so then I withdrew these people from Sanski Most as well. That is to say, they went home. So there were no soldiers providing any kind of security including at various points in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Whose arms depot was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you something else from this same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, we need page 2 and in B/C/S page 3. We need paragraph 4 now on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, it was stated here as far as disarming paramilitary formations in Sanski Most is concerned, as for the practical aspect it is Colonel Basara and Colonel Anicic that are charged with putting this into practice. Yesterday you said that did you not have any joint actions with Colonel Anicic with regard to this matter but now I'm going to ask you something about the first and the second conclusions. Did you receive these conclusions from the Crisis Staff? Were you given these conclusions to carry out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive these conclusions. I was not aware of them, so I don't even know the time when they adopted this. Anicic did not come to see me so that we would organise some kind of concerted action or anything like that. So I did everything according to my own plan and my own tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now just briefly in relation to Mahala. Yesterday my colleague Mr. Jeremy asked you whether you knew that civilians had lost their lives in Mahala, and your answer was yes. That is recorded on transcript page 34496. This is what I'm interested in. What do you know about this? Tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a few people lost their lives while combat was taking place. As for accurate information as to how many there were, I don't know. Where there is combat, where weapons are being fired, it is only natural that people will lose their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly take a look at P7322.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is your interview, and I would like us to take look at page 107, which happened to appear on our screens yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The 65 ter number is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Yesterday we were looking at the English version, page 108, and the B/C/S version, page 134. So now I'd like to ask that we take a look at the previous pages. So 107 in the English version, and 130 ... I think 133. [In English] We have to go one page back, please, in B/C/S. Now, in English, 107. In B/C/S, one page back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have been on the right page in B/C/S previously. 133.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now it's line 18 in B/C/S, and it's line 3 in English version on the pages we have on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said there what happened around the mosques, and this is what you say -- actually, I shouldn't read this out to you. What did you do, if anything, in order to protect religious buildings in the territory where your army was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ordered all battalion commanders to secure all religious buildings within the areas of responsibility of their units and that they should assign a certain number of men to guard them. That's what they did. However, what would happen was that during the night, armed people - no one could ever establish who that was - they would come from the dark and threaten these people who were guarding the religious facilities, saying that they would kill them if they wouldn't withdraw and, of course, they would withdraw because nobody was prepared to get killed either for a church or for a mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... finish in ten minutes. Do you want me to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can continue in ten minutes and if Mr. Mladic would agree that you continue now for another ten minutes, but then, of course, it's -- the Chamber does not oppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll continue, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague Mr. Jeremy yesterday mentioned the Prosecution witness when speaking of the killings at the Vrhpolje bridge. 147 is the page reference and 169 of our transcript. I think this is a mistake. I think it should say 2147 through 2169. Now, I'm going to read out something to you, something that a Prosecution witnesses, Raif Begic, said about this incident and then I'm going to put a question to you. On transcript page in this case 2199, lines 18 through 23, I quote: [In English] "Q. And then you go on to say that you were beaten by Chetniks on the bridge. What kind of insignia did they have, if you remember? "A. They had different insignia. Like I said, some were wearing military uniforms, some were wearing blue uniforms, some had Chetnik insignia. Some had just regular items of clothing, waist-coats, jackets, so it was all mixed." [Interpretation] My question, Mr. Basara, the soldiers of the 6th Krajina Brigade were they dressed this way? Did they wear such insignia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Members of the 6th Krajina Brigade all had uniforms and they all wore insignia. Later when Republika Srpska was declared, then the insignia of Republika Srpska. Before that some of them had five-pointed stars and others did not have any insignia. I saw soldiers and no one wore Chetnik insignia, cockades or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the 31st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, they did not have any other insignia. Someone could have had the five-pointed red star if it already been sewn into the cap they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there members of your brigade who had a blue uniform or moved about in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not have any blue uniforms or civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'd also like to direct the Chamber's attention to read the transcript page 2202 in this case, lines 17 through 23, where the witness said that, according to his opinion, on that occasion, the people involved were not members of the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked about P7323.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can have it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is a criminal report you signed against Danilusko Kajtez. Who drafted such documents in your brigade, documents of this type?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents of this type were drafted by the security organ as well as the assistance commander for morale and training.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Danilusko Kajtez was arrested and if he was arrested by whom?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who arrested him. I only know that I signed the order and the competent organs followed it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me briefly ask you about SOS units. You mentioned Njunja. What was his name, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know him as Njunja. Perhaps his last name was Savovic and his first name Dusan or something like that. Aka Njunja.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I told you his name was Dusan Saovic, does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my mind, it is Savovic; but I don't know if it is Saovic or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were he and the members of his unit under your command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not under my command but when the VRS was established we tried, I made an effort, to place them under brigade command so that I could exercise control over their activities. However, it was difficult to achieve because sometimes they accepted it and then at other times they withdrew, so you never knew whether they truly accepted the command of the brigade or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they report to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing whatsoever. Njunja did things of his own accord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking at audible volume. Please proceed. It is not for you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara. Thank you. I apologise for the additional time we spent torturing you. Thank you again for answering our questions. This would be all.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Jeremy, could you give us an indication as to how much time would you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't have any re-cross. The only outstanding issue, as I see it, is the diary P7321 MFI. Given the time pressure that we're experiencing with the videolink, then my suggestion would be that I make a short written submission on this or, if the Court prefers, I would follow up with an oral submission after the videolinks this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't need the witness for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one or two questions for the witness. I also noted that the next witness would be available in the videolink only at half past 11.00. So, therefore, I suggest we take the break and that after that break I put my one or two questions to the witness, and then we ... I pushed you very much. I didn't know at the time, Mr. Lukic, when I said one hour we would look at it, I didn't have that information yet that the next witness would be available or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We didn't consult you. We calculated my time without having the ruling from -- by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take the break first. We'll take the break. The witness is not excused yet, although he will likely be excused soon after the break. We now take a break and we resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, you were questioned about a meeting where it was recorded that General Talic was present and then you said, Well, you don't remember that General Talic was there but you seemed to remember that there was a Lieutenant-Colonel Mustafa Talic who would, instead, have been attending. Could you tell us in what capacity Lieutenant-Colonel Mustafa Talic would have attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, he happened to be there by chance. He came to the municipal building and the meeting took place at that time. He participated in the meeting, he even contributed, although I can't remember exactly what he said now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're telling us that someone was there by chance and then he joins the meeting and contributes, and that's all coincidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Rasula and others accepted officers at times. He was in uniform, and when he arrived, they simply took him as such: An officer, lieutenant-colonel, who sat in the meeting. As far as I remember, he also discussed some things, although I can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't remember what his contribution was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the fact that it's twice mentioned in the document that it was General Talic, do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I can't explain who wrote it. As far as I recall, I don't remember Talic being there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean General Talic or do you mean Lieutenant-Colonel Talic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, general. General Talic. I had him in mind. I don't remember him coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, he would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation as -- as the -- that your statements are -- well, not very consistent in this respect over the years?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of statements I provided about that, but I don't think it was previously put to me that General Talic was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We -- we have looked at the previous statements. I have another question for you about the demolition of the mosques. Was there any report in writing on your people trying to protect the mosques and then at night being chased away by unknown persons who then demolished the mosques, apart from that one mosque which was ordered to be destroyed? Did you write any reports about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not write a single report of that kind because the brigade command did not ask for any such reports. Since there was no state of war, one could not force those securing a facility to be killed over a mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But if you give a task to protect mosques and then they're all destroyed, isn't that an important matter which should be reported, that the security situation was such that it should be known by the higher-up levels?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, such information was not requested at all by the command. What was requested was the manning levels and casualties. As for the buildings and how many houses were destroyed in operations, or religious buildings, such information was not requested, and we did not provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You did not consider it of sufficient relevance? Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can understand it any which way you want, but that was the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now I would like to take you back to P2414 which was shown to you by Mr. Lukic. Could we have it on our screens. Mr. Lukic drew your attention to paragraph 6 of these conclusions of the 8th of June of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most. I'd like to draw your attention to number 2. Could you please read that for yourself and tell me when you are done.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read item 2. However, I am not familiar with it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and Nenad Davidovic did not inform me of this in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you agree that this is another example, apart from the ones that we saw already, that at least the Crisis Staff thinks that there is co-operation between the 6th Brigade Command and the Civil Defence Staff and that they should co-operate in preparations such as here, the Vrhpolje-Hrustovo theatre to be cleared. Do you agree that this is another example where such co-operation can mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Co-operation is mentioned, but since the municipality had all of its bodies in place, under the law we worked under, which was the Law on All People's Defence, the sanitization and hygiene measures in the field are carried out exclusively by units of civilian protection. There was no need for me to take part in it because there was no significant combat activity which may have resulted in a significant number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Had you attended the meeting of the 8th of June, 1992 of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't tell you anything about dates in terms of when I attended something and when I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm seeking the assistance of the parties to see whether the -- there are any minutes or notebooks that give more -- a better view on the attendance. Witness, I have the following question for you. We've seen repeatedly that in these documents it's described how you should or would co-operate, co-ordinate, in whatever way, and your answers persistently say that it was all not what really happened. Do you have any explanation as why they would continue and repeatedly give instructions how to co-operate with the 6th Brigade where you say it never happened? I mean, isn't -- doesn't there come a moment when one should realise that such co-operation was useless to even think of because it wasn't done anyhow, ever?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such co-operation to the extent referred to in the documents did not exist. Why they kept repeating it and asking for it without forwarding those decisions to the brigade command is something that we should ask the people from the municipal organs and from the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever thought that perhaps the 6th Brigade, as such, was not attending any meetings but it was just you as a person, though being commander of the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many times I have said so far why. As the commander I participated at the meetings of the municipal -- of the Muslim municipality when there was division. I also attended the sessions of the Serbian Assembly, and I wanted to know at any time what the intentions of both sides were. That is why I attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm talking about the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality, not about assembly meetings.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say municipal assembly meetings but when they separated, I also attended the meetings of the Muslim authorities. If they registered me in their documents, one would also be able, perhaps, to say that I was a member of their Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I leave it to that. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but Judge Fluegge has one question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, I would like to take you back to the event on the Vrhpolje bridge. You told us that you didn't know the perpetrators. Have you got any information in the meantime who the perpetrators were?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never received any information. Such information was not available because it was a civil war. It was very difficult to apprehend perpetrators wherever they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we knew who the perpetrators of a particular crime were, we always made sure that procedure was initiated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last sentence of paragraph 44 of your statement you say, I quote: "I found out that the perpetrators of these murders were some people from Kljuc." What's the basis for this information.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information and my conclusion is based on the fact that those people fled in the area -- direction of Kljuc territory. The people at the check-point in Sanski Most claimed that they didn't know them and that they did not hail from the territory of Sanski Most, from some of the villages whose inhabitants they knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You're saying that they fled in that direction?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They fled in that direction. They didn't stay there. It's not that I could have spoken to them. When they heard Colonel Basara, they simply fled in the direction of Kljuc. There are a few houses there, as far as I can remember, and nobody could have stopped them although these other people were shouting that they should stop, but they simply fled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you are, indeed, saying in this -- in your statement that there were some people from Kljuc, and you concluded that only from the information that they fled in that direction; is that correct? No other sources.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Statements of the men who were there at the check-point who are from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've just I'd like to return to the -- this meeting on the 20th of April. Could we take a look at P3294; and that's Mr. Rasula's diary. If we could go to page 25 in the English and page 21 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Basara, I'd like to focus your attention on the right side of the page in the B/C/S at the bottom of that page, and these are the minutes of that meeting on the 20th of April, 1992. Now, you've -- you've just said that that you didn't -- that contrary to your previous testimony in Stanisic and Zupljanin case you said that you thought a Lieutenant-Colonel Mustafa Talic was present at this meeting. He happened to be wandering past the municipal assembly and he came in and attended this meeting. Now, we see here that comments are attributed to a General Talic and they are concluding remarks. We see this reference to reach agreement but without undue delay. The military police from Prijedor shall remain and if need be from Banja Luka do not recognise paramilitary formations and a reference to barricades being put up. Can you explain why if Lieutenant-Colonel Mustafa Talic just happened to be wandering past and came into this meeting he would be given the floor to provide the concluding remarks for this meeting of the leading ethnicities -- ethnic representatives in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you misunderstood me. I was claiming that I did not remember, that I did not remember, what this lieutenant-colonel said. I don't remember the date when this meeting was held. So I can just claim that I don't remember that, that meeting. Maybe it did take place, but I don't remember it. I don't remember how it went, that meeting, I don't remember the conclusions ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave it there. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question in this respect. You nevertheless were able to tell me how it happened that Lieutenant-Colonel Mustafa Talic, how he attended that meeting, and now you are telling us that you don't have any recollection about the meeting. By the way, which, you, at some time in the past did as well. Could you explain why you could give me those details and though not having any recollection about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, thinking about that, trying to remember whether General Talic was there or not, I remembered that several times this Lieutenant-Colonel Talic, Mustafa Talic - I'm not sure that that's his first name, though - and he talked to me several times and he attended certain meetings at the municipality. However, I don't remember which ones so that I could tell you specifically on such and such a date, et cetera. So this is just a superficial memory. I am not asserting anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from General Talic was not present, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm saying I'm not asserting that because I don't know because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. While we are on this page --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Basara, let me just ask you this: Colonel Hasotic is mentioned here above General Talic. Do you know who Colonel Hasotic is, is he from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this does not arise from my question. It was mainly it was Talic, General, or Talic Lieutenant-Colonel, that was the issue raised, and, therefore, we are not going to revisit the whole of the document also in respects not raised before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only, Your Honour, only Mr. Basara said that these people from Crisis Staff would accept officers who were not from Sanski Most if they visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He wasn't -- I think he wasn't asked that. He was only asked about Talic. But put that question. We'll hear the answer, and then conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that he --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Basara, do you know what the ethnicity is of Colonel Hasotic and where he came from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Hasotic is a Muslim. That I know. And I think that he came from Banja Luka. Maybe ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just what you know. Thank you. That's all that we had. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you to the Court for having allowed these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the English version, it's Colonel Hasagic. The handwriting in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Should be Hasotic, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not clear the handwriting in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be some confusion there. Witness, I'd like to thank you very much for coming to the place of the videolink. I'd like to thank you for having answered the questions that were put to you, questions put to you by the parties, questions put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar at the other side of the videolink, could the next witness be escorted in the videolink room.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, will it be you who will examine the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next witness you call is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Grujo Boric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Boric. Before you give evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boric. Please be seated. Mr. Boric, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. But before we continue, I took it from your answer that you're able to see us and to hear us in a language you understand. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Your Honour, I'd expected to have a moment before the witness was brought in, but just in view of the questions that are likely to be asked and the witness's position, we'd ask that he be informed of his rights under Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll do so, Mr. Stojanovic, unless you think that your questions are not such that it makes sense at all. And it is because it is viva voce evidence that we do not know which questions you will put to the witness. If you ask him about the weather there may be no need to do it but if there are any questions which expose the witness to any risk, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. So I have no problem with you addressing him on that, the rule, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking this, Mr. Traldi, because it's usually the calling party who knows what questions will you put and that's -- they consider it. But in view of the answer given by Mr. Stojanovic, I'll put the following to the witness. Mr. Boric, Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence have the following text and I'll read it slowly to you: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Mr. Boric, if, therefore, you have concerns that a truthful answer to any of the questions might incriminate yourself or might tend to incriminate yourself, don't hesitate to address me and ask to be relieved from answering that question. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Boric. Welcome.

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: Good day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the procedure existing here, could you please tell us your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: Grujo Boric. Father's name Milko [phoen]. Mother's name Grozda [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: The 12th of July, 1938, village of Kandici, municipality of Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, where do you live today, General, sir?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: I live in Novi Sad, Bulevar Oslobodjenje number 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber about your education and your career until you retired.

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: I completed the secondary military school in 1956. The Military Academy in 1992. The higher Military Academy and the War School in Belgrade in 1971 -- 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, please, could you repeat the year when you completed the Military Academy?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: The Military Academy? I graduated from the Military Academy in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell the Trial Chamber which duties you held in 1990 and 1991 at the time when the war broke out in the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: I was chief of the 6th Lika Division in Karlovac; commander of the 7th Banja Division in Petrinja; Chief of Staff of defence of Zagreb; and assistant for logistics of the 10th Corps in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were the tasks of the then-JNA in Croatia, following the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: There was much tension because the Croatians were looking to secede, to become independent. This caused clashes between Croats and Serbs and in those situations, we served as a buffer. When the clash at Plitvice took place, I personally participated in creating this buffer zone with my unit. Later on, when the conflict moved to Banja in Glina, I was present there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until when did you remain in the territory of the Republic of Croatia as a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: Until May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court where was your unit dislocated at the time, including yourself?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: I was in Glina until part of the command and some units of the 10th Corps left Zagreb. After that, I arrived in Bihac. There, I joined the command of the 10th Corps in Bihac. It was in late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of situation did you encounter in Bosnia and Herzegovina, specifically in the area of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: There was a clash between Serbs and Croats in Bihac. 90 per cent of Serbs left Bihac. Even barracks were attacked and a guard of ours was killed. Close to Bihac, there was an airport which, at the time, was still under JNA control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, between December 1991 and the summer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were the specific tasks that you and your unit of the JNA had which you received from your superior command?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: When the corps command arrived in Bihac, the 10th Corps was joined by the units at Samarica, Drinska Gora, and Plitvice. These were the units which had already been sent to the front line, as well as some territorial units which happened to be in the territory of Bihac. The units which had previously been assigned to the front lines had their task to maintain the lines there. On the other hand, wherever there were incidents and clashes, we tried to reduce tensions and to separate Muslim and Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As a superior officer, did you have any personal knowledge about the illegal arming of the population at the time?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: While we were still in Zagreb, there was the Spegelj affair, who commanded the Croatian TO. He was importing weapons from Hungary, illegally, distributing those weapons to the Croatian population. However his trial was prevented from taking place by Croatian authorities and the population in Zagreb. Neither he nor his group were ever convicted. In any case, people were being armed everywhere, including Muslims and Serbs in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, did JNA units have specific problems with the population of Bihac and their stay in the military facilities in the area of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: We were frequently attacked. Members of the Green Berets, their groups, organised or set up specific points along different routes, stopping columns of vehicles moving towards Petrovac and further afield. For the most part, Serbs left the territory of Bihac en masse. I can say that at the time 15 officers arrived in Bihac. They were officers and non-commissioned officers of Muslim ethnicity. They were transferred there which seemed odd in view of the fact that the situation was difficult and that they were not to remain in the unit. I spoke with all of them and asked them if they were prepared to fight, should we be attacked by the population of Bihac municipality, given that some of them had their families in the town. 90 per cent of them answered negatively. We paid them out and let them join their families in the town. Only one warrant officer remained, by the name of Peskir [phoen], I think, and a second lieutenant, they were both of Muslim ethnicity. The latter remained in the police and later he, too, joined its ranks and joined his family in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until what time did the corps remain in Bihac and the barracks there?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: Around the 19th of May, 1992, an order was issued that the officers and soldiers born in Montenegro, Macedonia and Serbia were to leave the territory of Bosnia for Serbia. Those officers hailing from Bosnia, if they wished so, were free to stay or to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your decision, given your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: I received an order on my appointment as the Chief of Staff of the 10th Corps which was already in the process of disintegration as the officers from Serbia and Montenegro were already leaving. Some 250 soldiers hailing from Bosnia remained, together with some 20 officers. I assembled them all, explained the situation, and they all accepted to stay with me and with the officers to fight alongside our own people in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you stay physically in the Bihac town at that time?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: We received an order to leave Bihac. At the time, the airport had been destroyed; one part of it. All the preparations had been made to leave Bihac. The president of the municipality made arrangements about that with me in person. Around the 20th or 22nd May 1992, we left the whole command and all materiel that had been stored in the depots in Bihac, moved to the territory of Petrovac municipality, to Krnjeusa village and the commands accommodated itself at a school there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any conflicts with paramilitary formations which you called the Green Berets during this period?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: We departed from Bihac in an organised manner. The president of the municipality was in the car with me, and when we left, we said farewells at the border of Bihac municipality and we left. We had no problems at all. But the second lieutenant of Muslim ethnicity was the commander of a military police unit. He took a combat vehicle. He let the soldiers leave and then he drove off the vehicle to Bihac. I later heard that he was killed. I got in touch with the president of the municipality as we were in telephone communication. We had radio sets, that is to say. I asked him to have the vehicle returned but he did not manage to achieve that. I would tell you a few words about the president of the municipality of Bihac. His first name was Serbian. As he was a Muslim when I asked him how come his first name was Serbian, he said that his father had served the army in the JNA in Sumadija. He had a good friend there and they agreed that if they would have sons, that they would give them their respective names. That was why the president of the municipality was not much loved by the Muslims. I later heard that he was killed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell us when it was that you received the information about the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska, if you received that information, that is?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: I told you that the command left for the general sector of Petrovac to Krnjeusa village. I met General Mladic in Drvar at his request. He came there together with a colleague, General Savo Kovacevic, and I was told that a corps would be formed and that we would receive an order and that I would most probably be appointed commander of this corps. That was on the 25th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive such an order on your appointment as corps commander at any point?

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: I received a decree from President Karadzic rather than an order. That was around the month of July 1992. In early July; I think it may have been the 7th or the 8th of July. I was appointed commander of the 2nd Krajina Corps. Colonel Mico Vlaisavljevic was appointed as Chief of Staff. Both of us were colonels at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please describe to the Chamber the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps at the moment when you took over the command of this corps.

utterances.speaker: GRUJO BORIC
utterances.text: The zone was vast. The front was 200-odd kilometres, all the way from Krupa Na Uni to Petrovac, Bihac, Drvar, Grahovo, Glamoc, Kupres. In depth Sipovo, Kljuc and Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is there any dispute about the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps? That's one. Have you tried to see whether there is -- and if there's a difference, does that affect in any specific way other disputes between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll actually ask that the witness remove headphones for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you please take off your headphones. But, witness, could you -- no, I think if he has no headphones he wouldn't hear anything. It's videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But he'll take off his headphones anyhow. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, actually based on the witness's answer and the specific way Mr. Stojanovic formulated the question, there is a dispute about the accuracy of the answer the witness gave. There -- one of the municipalities according to evidence the Chamber has received that he mentioned wasn't part of the zone of responsibility at the moment when he took over the commands of the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not because I interrupted him that he had not finished his list yet? Is that a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
